    theme(

# options(tinytable_html_mathjax = TRUE)

# Data -------------------------------------------------------------------------
coffee <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data/coffee.csv")) |>
  mutate(

## Plan for today

- Explain the one-way ANOVA model and its assumptions.
- Estimate group means using least squares.
- Explain how the ANOVA F-test compares between-group and within-group variation.
- Represent a categorical predictor using dummy variables.
- Express one-way ANOVA as a multiple linear regression model.
- Interpret the coefficients from different regression parameterisations.
- Fit and interpret a one-way ANOVA model in R.

## Let's take an example

A study was carried out to examine the effects of caffeine on unrest.

Thirty students were randomly assigned to one of three groups:

- Control: no caffeine.
- Caffeine: low dose of caffeine.
- Caffeine + sugar: low dose of caffeine with sugar.

::: {.callout-note}
## Research question

Is there evidence that mean unrest differs between the three groups?
:::

## Let's take an example

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-1
coffee |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = x, fill = x)) +
  gghalves::geom_half_point(
    transformation = ggbeeswarm::position_quasirandom(),
    side = "l"
  ) +
  gghalves::geom_half_boxplot(side = "r", colour = "black") +
  ggokabeito::scale_colour_okabe_ito() +
  ggokabeito::scale_fill_okabe_ito() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean unrest") +
  guides(colour = "none", fill = "none") +
  theme_st303()
```

## One-way ANOVA model {style="font-size: 85%;"}

One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares the population means of two or
more independent groups.

We have:

- One categorical variable: treatment group.
- One continuous variable: unrest score.
- Three treatment groups.

We can define:

- $g$ denote the number of groups
- $n_i$ denote the number of observations in group $i$.
- $Y_{ij}$ denote the response for person $j$ in group $i$.

## One-way ANOVA model {style="font-size: 70%;"}

### The means model

The one-way ANOVA model can be written as:

$$
\boxed{
  Y_{ij} = \mu_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij} \quad \varepsilon \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathcal{N(0, \sigma^2)}
}
$$

- $\mu_i$ is the population mean for group $i$.
- $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is the random error for person $j$ in group $i$.


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

For three groups, the model is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
  Y_{1j}&=\mu_1+\varepsilon_{1j}\\
  Y_{2j}&=\mu_2+\varepsilon_{2j}\\
  Y_{3j}&=\mu_3+\varepsilon_{3j}
\end{aligned}
$$

We estimate the unknown group means using ordinary least squares.

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{g} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (Y_{ij}-\mu_i)^2
$$

:::

## One-way ANOVA model {style="font-size: 70%;"}

### Ordinary least squares

$$
\boxed{\sum_{i=1}^{g} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (Y_{ij}-\mu_i)^2}
$$

Because each group has its own mean, we can minimise the sum of squares
for each group.


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_i(\mu_i) &= \sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(Y_{ij}-\mu_i)^2 \\[4pt]
&= -2\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(Y_{ij}-\mu_i) \\[4pt]
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&0 = \sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(Y_{ij}-\hat{\mu}_i) \\[4pt]
&\hat{\mu_i} = \sum^{n_i}_{j = 1} \frac{Y_{ij}}{n_i} = \bar{Y}_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

:::

With some rearranging we get

$$
\boxed{\hat{\mu}_i = \bar{Y}_{i}}
$$


::: {.callout-important}
## The OLS estimate of each group mean is simply the sample mean for that group.
:::

## The coffee data {style="font-size: 85%;"}

The fitted value for an individual is the mean of the group to which they belong:

$$
\hat{Y}_{ij} = \hat{\mu}_i = \bar{Y}_{i}
$$

<br>


::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="33%"}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-2a
coffee |>
  group_by(x) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(y) |> round(2)) |>
  rename(`Treatment group` = x, `Mean Unrest` = mean) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```

:::

::: {.column width="66%"}

```{r}
#| label: chunk-2b
coffee |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(group = x),
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    shape = 23,
    size = 5,
    fill = "orange"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Unrest score",
  ) +
  theme_st303()
```

:::

:::

## Testing whether group means differ

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_0&:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_g \\[4pt]
H_A&:\text{not all population means are equal}
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
The alternative does not require every group mean to differ.
It only requires at least one difference.
:::

::::: {.fragment}

We can break this difference down into two components


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

[**Between-group variation**]{.center}

$$
SSG=\sum_{i=1}^{g} n_i(\bar{Y}_{i}-\bar{Y})^2
$$

:::

::: {.column}

[**Within-group variation**]{.center}

$$
SSE= \sum_{i=1}^{g} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (Y_{ij}-\bar{Y}_{i})^2
$$

:::

::::
:::::

## {style="font-size: 80%;"}

<br>


```{r}
#| label: chunk-3
ggplot(coffee, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(group = x),
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    shape = 23,
    size = 5,
    fill = "orange"
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(group = x),
    fun = mean,
    geom = "line",
    linewidth = 1,
    colour = "orange"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = mean(coffee$y),
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Unrest score",
  ) +
  theme_st303()
```

- **Between-group variation** reflects differences
  [between the group means]{.alert}.
- **Within-group variation** reflects differences
  [between individuals in the same group]{.alert}.

## The ANOVA table {style="font-size: 95%;"}

We can summarise all of this information in an ANOVA table

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-4
tribble(
  ~Source , ~df   , ~SS   , ~MS               , ~F        ,
  "Group" , "g-1" , "SSG" , "MSG = SSG/(g-1)" , "MSG/MSE" ,
  "Error" , "n-g" , "SSE" , "MSE = SSE/(n-g)" , ""        ,
  "Total" , "n-1" , "SST" , ""                , ""
) |>
  tt(width = c(0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.2)) |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```

Where

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- $SSG=\sum_{i=1}^{g} n_i(\bar{Y}_{i}-\bar{Y})^2$
- $SSE= \sum_{i=1}^{g} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (Y_{ij}-\bar{Y}_{i})^2$
- $SST= \sum_{i=1}^{g} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (Y_{ij}-\bar{Y})^2$

:::

::: {.column}

[Under the null hypothesis:]{.center}

$$
F_{\text{obs}}\sim F_{g-1,n-g}
$$

[We reject the null for sufficiently large values of the F-statistic]{.center}

:::

::::

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Moving from groups to predictors

So far, we have described the three groups using three population means:

$$
\mu_1,\qquad\mu_2,\qquad\mu_3
$$

But multiple regression allows us to represent categorical explanatory
variables using dummy variables.

A dummy variable is an indicator variable taking the value:

$$
X_i=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if the observation belongs to group }i\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

For three groups, we define:

$$
X_1,\qquad X_2,\qquad X_3.
$$

Each observation belongs to exactly one group.

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Moving from groups to predictors

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-5
tribble(
  ~Group             , ~`$X_1$` , ~`$X_2$` , ~`$X_3$` ,
  "Control"          ,        1 ,        0 ,        0 ,
  "Caffeine"         ,        0 ,        1 ,        0 ,
  "Ceffeine & Sugar" ,        0 ,        0 ,        1
) |>
  tt()
```


For every observation:

$$
X_1 + X_2 + X_3 = 1
$$

These three dummy variables completely identify group membership.

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### The regression model

Using the three dummy variables, we can write:

$$
Y_j=\mu_1X_{1j}+\mu_2X_{2j}+\mu_3X_{3j}+\varepsilon_j
$$

::::: {.fragment .fade-up}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}

### Control group {.center}

$$Y_j=\mu_1+\epsilon_j$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

### Caffeine group {.center}

$$Y_j=\mu_2+\epsilon_j$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

### Caffeine + sugar group {.center}

$$Y_j=\mu_3+\epsilon_j$$

:::

::::
:::::


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Or in matrix form

$$
\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} +\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \qquad \qquad
\boldsymbol{\mu}= \begin{bmatrix}
\mu_1 \\ \mu_2 \\ \mu_3
\end{bmatrix} \qquad \qquad
\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
1&0&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
0&1&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
0&0&1\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Ordinary least squares

$$
\boxed{\hat{\mu} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{Y}}
$$

For the means model, each observation belongs to only one group. Therefore:

$$
\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix}
n_1&0&0\\
0&n_2&0\\
0&0&n_3
\end{bmatrix} \qquad
\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{Y} = \begin{bmatrix}
\sum_jY_{1j}\\
\sum_jY_{2j}\\
\sum_jY_{3j}
\end{bmatrix} \qquad \text{where} \; \; (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
1/n_1&0&0\\
0&1/n_2&0\\
0&0&1/n_3
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Thus

$$
\boldsymbol{\hat{\mu}} =
\frac{1}{n_i} \mathbf{I}_3 \begin{bmatrix} Y_1 \\ Y_2 \\ Y_3\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\bar{Y}_{1}\\
\bar{Y}_{2}\\
\bar{Y}_{3}
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}
\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{1}\\
\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{2}\\
\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{3}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 75%;"}

### Fitted values and residuals

Once we have estimated the group means, we can calculate the fitted values and
residuals.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

### Fitted values {.center}

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

### Residual {.center}

$$
\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{Y} - \widehat{\mathbf{Y}}
$$

:::
::::

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
In a one-way ANOVA, **the fitted value for each observation is simply the
estimated mean of the group to which that observation belongs**.
:::

::::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Let's suppose that:

$$
\widehat{\mu}_1=244.80,\qquad
\widehat{\mu}_2=246.40,\qquad
\widehat{\mu}_3=248.30
$$

Hence, for an individual in the caffeine group with an unrest score of 250.00

<br>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

### Fitted value {.center}

$$
\widehat{Y} = 246.40
$$

:::

::: {.column}

### Residual {.center}

$$
e = 250 - 246.40 = 3.60
$$

:::
::::
:::::

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Where's the intercept

An [alternative regression model]{.alert} is:

$$
Y_j = \mu + \alpha_1X_{1j} + \alpha_2X_{2j} + \alpha_3X_{3j} + \epsilon_j
$$


::: {.callout-note}
## This is called an effects model
:::


However, we need to remember that

$$
X_1 + X_2 + X_3 = 1
$$

The intercept column is therefore exactly equal to the sum of the three
dummy-variable columns

This means that the design matrix is not of full column rank

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Where's the intercept

$$
\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{bmatrix}
1&1&0&0\\
1&1&0&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
1& 0&1&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
1&0&0&1\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots
\end{bmatrix}
$$


::: {.callout-important}

## Why is this a problem?

If we include an intercept and all three dummy variables, there is
perfect linear dependence between the columns of the design matrix.

Consequently $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is singular and cannot be inverted

There is no unique estimate of all four coefficients.

[This is called perfect multicollinearity or the dummy-variable trap.]{.alert}

:::

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Where's the intercept

We can solve this in one of two ways

<br>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

### Method 1 {.center}

Keep the means model

$$
Y_j=\mu_1X_{1j}+\mu_2X_{2j}+\mu_3X_{3j}+\epsilon_j
$$

:::

::: {.column}

### Method 2 {.center}

Treat the control $n_1$ as the reference group

$$
Y_j= \mu+ \alpha_2X_{2j} + \alpha_3X_{3j} + \epsilon_j
$$

:::
::::


::::: {.fragment .fade-up}

$$\boxed{Y_j= \mu+ \alpha_2X_{2j} + \alpha_3X_{3j} + \epsilon_j}$$



:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Control} &\qquad \mu \\[4pt]
\text{Caffeine} &\qquad \mu - \alpha_2 \\[4pt]
\text{Caffeine + Sugar} &\qquad \mu - \alpha_3
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu&=\mu_1\\
\alpha_2&=\mu_2-\mu_1\\
\alpha_3&=\mu_3-\mu_1
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::
:::::

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Linear contrasts (how to compare groups)

Sometimes we are interested in comparisons involving more than two group means.

For example, suppose we want to compare the mean unrest score in the
control group with the average of the caffeine and caffeine + sugar groups.

$$
L = \mu_1 - \frac{1}{2}\mu_2 - \frac{1}{2}\mu_3
$$


::: {.fragment .fade-up}
More generally, a linear contrast is a linear combination of
population group means with a set of contrast coefficients:
$\mathbf{c} = (c_1, c_2, \dots, c_k)^\top$, where $\sum^k_{i=1} c_k = 0$

$$
L = c_1\mu_1+c_2\mu_2+\cdots+c_k\mu_k,
$$

In our example, these coefficients are

$$
\mathbf{c} = (1, \; -\frac{1}{2}, \; -\frac{1}{2})^\top
$$

:::

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Linear contrasts (how to compare groups)

We can estimate a linear contrast by replacing the population means with
their least-squares estimates.

For our contrast

$$
\begin{aligned}
L &= \widehat{\mu}_1 - \frac{1}{2}\widehat{\mu}_2 - \frac{1}{2}\widehat{\mu}_3 \\[4pt]
&= 244.80 - \frac{1}{2}(246.40) - \frac{1}{2} 248.30 \\[4pt]
&= 244.80 - 247.35 \\[4pt]
&= -2.55
\end{aligned}
$$


::: {.callout-tip}
## Interpretation

The estimated mean unrest score in the control group is approximately 2.55
lower than the equally weighted average of the caffeine and caffeine +
sugar group
:::

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 75%;"}

### Linear contrasts (standard errors)

Recall that the variance–covariance matrix of the least-squares estimates is:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}) =
\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}
$$

A linear contrast can be written in matrix notation as:

$$
\widehat{L} = \mathbf{c}^{\mathsf T} \; \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
$$

Its estimated variance is therefore:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat{L})
=
\widehat{\sigma}^2 \;
\mathbf{c}^{\mathsf T} \;
(\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{c}
$$

Taking the square root gives the standard error:

$$
\boxed{
SE(\widehat{L})=
\sqrt{
\widehat{\sigma}^2 \;
\mathbf{c}^{\mathsf T} \;
(\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{c}
}
}
$$

This allows us to quantify the uncertainty associated with our estimated
contrast.

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 75%;"}

### Linear contrasts (standard errors)

For our linear contrast we can say that

$$
\sigma^2 = 4.968 \qquad \text{and} \qquad
(\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X})^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
1/10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1/10
\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{10}\mathbf{I}_3
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{c}^{\mathsf T} \; (\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{c} =
\frac{1}{10} (1^2 - \frac{1}{2}^2 - \frac{1}{2}^2) = 0.15
$$

Hence

$$
SE(\widehat{L})= \sqrt{4.968 * 0.15} = 0.863
$$


## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Linear contrasts (hypothesis testing)

We can use a linear contrast to test whether a particular comparison of
population means differs from zero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_0: \mu_1 - \frac12\mu_2 - \frac12\mu_3 = 0 \\[4pt]
H_1: \mu_1 - \frac12\mu_2 - \frac12\mu_3 \ne 0
\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the following test statistic:

$$
t=\frac{\widehat{L}-0}{SE(\widehat{L})},
$$

which under the null hypothesis is assumed to follow a $t$-distribution with
degrees of freedom $N - g$

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 70%;"}

### Doing it in R

```{r}
#| label: chunk-6
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

# Fit an effects model
fit_1 <- lm(y ~ x, data = coffee)

# What is the output
summary(fit_1)

# What does the design matrix look like
model.matrix(fit_1) |> head()
```

## ANOVA as multiple regression {style="font-size: 70%;"}

### Doing it in R

```{r}
#| label: chunk-7
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

# Fit an means model
fit_2 <- lm(y ~ x - 1, data = coffee)

# What is the output
summary(fit_2)

# What does the design matrix look like
model.matrix(fit_2) |> head()
```
